# Run the rounding skill as a scheduled workflow {#sec-workflow-rounding-lab}

::: callout-tip
Build the skill first, test one run second, and install the schedule last. A cron
expression cannot compensate for an untested task contract.
:::

This lab implements the workflow designed in @sec-workflow-rounding-skill. It is
not a second workflow or another pass through the AI-first SDLC. The workflow
brief, task contract, benchmark, release record, and monitoring design remain in
that chapter. Here, the reader exercises their prototype counterparts.

The learning objective is practical: create a code-agent skill, invoke it on a
bounded R project, and connect it to a scheduled controller that reviews one
package per run. The controller rotates across five packages, skips unchanged
commits, and prepares one package-level GitHub issue containing all current
verified BR-001 findings.

::: {.callout-warning title="A safe default for a public book"}
The lab defaults to a dry run. It does not create, update, comment on, or close
an issue unless the operator explicitly enables publishing. Readers must not
enable publishing against repositories they do not administer or have
permission to automate. The five-package pilot requires maintainer authorization
and separate process-owner acceptance before every external issue action.
:::

## Inspect the working prototype

The prototype is under
[`exercise/rounding/`](exercise/rounding/README.md):

```text
exercise/rounding/
  .agents/skills/rounding-rule-review/
    SKILL.md
    references/br-001.md
    scripts/scan-rounding-calls.R
    scripts/scan-rounding-lib.R
    scripts/probe-tie-behavior.R
    assets/review-report-template.md
  expected/
  fixtures/
  schemas/review-report.schema.json
  scripts/run-rotation.R
  scripts/validate-report.R
  scripts/publish-issue.R
  scripts/rounding-workflow.R
  targets.json
  state.example.json
  cron.example
```

The skill and the surrounding workflow have different responsibilities. The
skill tells an agent how to inspect and reason about one checked-out package.
The controller selects the package and commit and independently runs the
catalog scanner. The report validator enforces the finding admission rule and
checks source evidence against that selected checkout. The publisher owns
GitHub issue mechanics after a human gate. The process owner governs the
complete system.

That separation is visible in the permissions:

| Component | Can do | Cannot do |
|---|---|---|
| External agent adapter in an independently approved boundary | Read the mounted checkout and immutable skill inputs, run local evidence scripts, produce JSON | Receive host credentials, unrelated host files, network access, or issue-write authority |
| Scheduled controller | Select one package, resolve a commit, run the scanner, manage rotation state, invoke an approved adapter | Decide that unsupported evidence is a finding |
| Report validator | Enforce required fields and minimum evidence | Interpret clinical intent |
| Issue publisher | Manage one automation-owned BR-001 issue per package after per-run acceptance | Change source or another identity's issue |
| Process owner | Approve the operating policy and each issue action, monitor results, restrict or stop the workflow | Transfer accountability to the agent |

## Create and inspect the skill

The required `SKILL.md` contains `name` and `description` frontmatter. Its name
matches the `rounding-rule-review` directory. The description distinguishes the
BR-001 repository review from general R review and from BR-002 or BR-003 work.
That distinction matters because code agents can use the description when
deciding whether a skill applies.

The remaining content is disclosed only when needed:

- `references/br-001.md` controls the rule, scope, comparison version, catalog,
  and finding admission rule.
- `scan-rounding-calls.R` creates the complete R-file inventory and the minimum
  catalog candidate list from R parse data.
- `probe-tie-behavior.R` produces repeatable evidence for direct `round()` and
  numeric `formatC()` calls.
- `review-report-template.md` shows the managed section that can appear in a
  package issue.

This structure follows the [Agent Skills
specification](https://agentskills.io/specification). As verified on 2026-09-06,
the official [Codex skill documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/codex/build-skills)
states that Codex discovers repository skills under `.agents/skills` and can
invoke a skill explicitly with `$skill-name`. The lab keeps the package in that
location, so launching Codex from `exercise/rounding/` makes it discoverable.

To use the same skill in another repository with Codex, copy the complete
`rounding-rule-review` directory into that repository's `.agents/skills/`
directory. For another code agent, retain the skill contents and follow that
product's current first-party installation instructions.

## Verify the deterministic foundation

Follow [`exercise/rounding/README.md`](exercise/rounding/README.md) to install
the pinned `cards` 0.9.0 comparison dependency. Then run the offline tests from
the lab directory:

```bash
Rscript tests/test-rounding-workflow.R
```

The benchmark recorded on 2026-09-08 passes 31 offline tests. They cover report
admission, source-evidence validation, evidence from both tie signs, scanner
identity, commit matching, failure rotation, publication reconciliation, issue
rendering, preservation of human issue text, cron initialization, and the
Quarto boundary between immutable assets and runtime data. The full result and
its limitations are in the
[`benchmark report`](exercise/rounding/expected/benchmark-report.md).

Run the catalog scanner directly against the violation fixture:

```bash
Rscript .agents/skills/rounding-rule-review/scripts/scan-rounding-calls.R \
  fixtures/violations/R
```

The expected result is one R file, two catalog candidates, and no parse errors.
The scanner reports candidates rather than findings. Only source context and an
executed probe can admit a candidate to the verified finding list.

Run the fixed probe:

```bash
Rscript .agents/skills/rounding-rule-review/scripts/probe-tie-behavior.R \
  round 1 -2.05,2.05
```

The probe compares the observed one-decimal results with `cards::round5()`
0.9.0. Both values diverge in the recorded environment. The script returns a
nonzero status because it found a divergence; that status is evidence, not a
broken lab command.

## Exercise change detection without network access

The controller needs state that persists across runs. Use a temporary directory
for the offline exercise:

```bash
rounding_tmp="$(mktemp -d)"
Rscript scripts/run-rotation.R \
  --registry fixtures/targets.json \
  --state "$rounding_tmp/state.json" \
  --runs-dir "$rounding_tmp/runs" \
  --observed-sha aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa \
  --local-target fixtures/violations \
  --report-input expected/violations-report.json
```

The first run validates the answer-key report and renders the issue action
without executing it. Run the same command again with the same temporary state.
The second run records `no-change` and skips the full review.

This small exercise demonstrates a central workflow distinction. The daily
schedule is the event that asks for attention. The changed commit is the rule
that decides whether verification work should begin.

## Connect an independently isolated code-agent adapter

The prototype does not enable its built-in Codex adapter. A read-only Codex
sandbox alone does not establish the credential-free operating-system boundary
required for untrusted repository content, so a run without `--report-input` or
`--agent-adapter` fails closed.

An approved external adapter receives a prompt path, JSON Schema path, and
report output path. It succeeds only when it writes one conforming JSON report.
The adapter must run in a credential-free operating-system context with only
the required checkout and immutable skill inputs readable and with network,
web, Model Context Protocol (MCP), app, and connector access disabled. Clearing
common GitHub environment variables is defense in depth, not that isolation
boundary.

After independently verifying those controls, run one package without
publishing:

```bash
Rscript scripts/run-rotation.R \
  --agent-adapter /absolute/path/to/isolated-adapter
```

The first run selects `Merck/r2rtf`, resolves its `master` branch to an exact
commit, and stores that SHA before the agent starts. Later runs rotate through
`Merck/metalite.ae`, `Merck/metalite`, `Merck/forestly`, and
`elong0527/r4csr`. Every result is attached to the commit resolved for that
specific run. This interface keeps the workflow contract stable while product
commands change; the repository does not claim that a named agent product
supplies the required isolation by itself.

## Install the 30-run rotation

The repository does not activate a scheduled workflow. Instead,
[`cron.example`](exercise/rounding/cron.example) contains an inactive daily
template. It initializes the private `var/` directory before opening its log
file and names a placeholder for the independently isolated adapter. Replace
every placeholder with an absolute path and install it under the scheduled
service identity.

One invocation handles one package. The state advances rotationally even after
a failed attempt so one package cannot block the other four. A failed package
does not receive a new `last_completed_sha`, so its unchanged commit is retried
on its next turn. The controller refuses to start a second overlapping run and
stops after 30 scheduled attempts.

The schedule therefore produces this pattern:

| Run | Package |
|---:|---|
| 1, 6, 11, 16, 21, 26 | `Merck/r2rtf` |
| 2, 7, 12, 17, 22, 27 | `Merck/metalite.ae` |
| 3, 8, 13, 18, 23, 28 | `Merck/metalite` |
| 4, 9, 14, 19, 24, 29 | `Merck/forestly` |
| 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 | `elong0527/r4csr` |

If the selected branch did not change, the run ends with a no-change record.
If it changed, the workflow reviews the complete configured R folder at the new
SHA rather than assuming that a source diff proves full coverage.

## Authorize package-level issues

Issue publication is a separate action after review, not an automatic
consequence of accepting the release policy. Before any release, the process
owner must configure the dedicated automation login, confirm the target
registry, obtain maintainer authorization for all five repositories, and grant
the identity only content-read and issue-write access. For every completed run,
the process owner must inspect the scanner evidence and report, classify the
findings, and explicitly accept or reject the proposed issue action.

Publishing remains off unless the accountable operator records that per-run
acceptance by passing `--publish` for the reviewed report. The deterministic
publisher then applies these rules:

1. Search open issues for the package-and-rule marker.
2. Create one issue containing all current verified findings when none exists.
3. Update only the automation-managed section when the issue exists.
4. Add a comment when editing the issue body is unavailable.
5. Close the issue after a complete later review shows all findings addressed.
6. Create a new linked issue when findings recur after closure.
7. Refuse to modify an issue created by another identity.

Unresolved candidates do not qualify for automatic posting. A clean package
with no open automated issue produces a run record but no issue.

The controller refuses `--publish` without a pre-reviewed `--report-input`.
The standalone publisher likewise requires `--source-directory` when
`--publish` is present, then rechecks the scanner inventory, source evidence,
clean checkout, and exact commit before any GitHub action.

## Review the monitoring evidence

The mutable `var/` directory contains campaign state and one directory for each
run. At the end of the month, the process owner uses those records to account
for all 30 events and answer:

- Did each package receive six review opportunities?
- Which commits changed, and which runs correctly skipped unchanged source?
- Which runs completed, failed, or stopped with unresolved evidence?
- Were any duplicate open issues created?
- Which issues were created, updated, commented on, or closed?
- What findings were rejected or missed during human review?
- What were the review burden, detection delay, latency, and cost?
- Should the workflow continue, change, be restricted, or retire?

The month-long result is operating evidence, not proof that the workflow is
validated, compliant, or suitable for another organization's intended use.
